title: Case 1: Faking your type to “pass” a personality test
text: Based on a Seattle Times article (2005). More and more employers use written personality tests to screen applicants and predict how new hires will perform – for jobs from accountant to sales manager. Applicants answer true/false items or rate statements from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”; items measure traits such as openness or emotional stability.

The tests are popular because research has linked specific traits to performance in specific jobs – calm, steady people make good supervisors and security officers, persistent people with a strong sense of self suit commission-based sales – and tests have proved at least as predictive as interviews or simulations.

Critics say the tests are easy to manipulate: in experiments, people score consistently higher on positive traits when they believe they are applying for a job than when asked to answer honestly. A researcher warns applicants that faking may get them a job they end up hating.

title: Case 2: Linking pay to performance at Safelite
text: Based on Lazear (2000). Safelite Glass, the largest US installer of car glass, moved its installers from an hourly wage to a piece rate – pay per glass unit installed – because management felt productivity was too low.

How a job runs: a customer calls the customer service department, which books mobile or in-store service; the system picks the first slot based on glass and technician availability, orders the glass from the warehouse and assigns a technician. The manager routes the jobs and prints schedules; warehouse staff pick and check the parts and load them for each technician; the technician checks the parts, loads the truck and drives to the customers.

The technician's job depends on others: scheduling errors, miscommunication and wrong or missing glass from the warehouse are common. Demand also fluctuates with miles driven and the weather – storms and hail cause sudden peaks.
